cases.excerpt: Data from 11 cohort studies in the BLadder cancer Epidemiology and Nutritional Determinants (BLEND) study, provided sufficient information on fat intake for a total of 2731 BC cases and 544 452 noncases, which yielded 5 400 168 person-years of follow-up.

effect_size.excerpt: Among women, an inverse association was observed between mono-unsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) and BC risk (HR comparing the highest with the lowest tertile: 0.73, 95% CI: 0.58-0.93, P-trend = .01).

studies.Study: Li G et al. (2025) [PMID: 40237627] — estimate 1 · Female
studies.Reference: Dietary Fatty Acids and Bladder Cancer Risk: Insights from the PLCO Cancer Screening Trial.
studies.Title: Dietary Fatty Acids and Bladder Cancer Risk: Insights from the PLCO Cancer Screening Trial.
studies.Authors: Li G, Zheng W, Zhang X, Chen Y
studies.comparison_type: Higher MUFA intake versus lower intake; exact categories not stated

cases.excerpt: During a median follow-up of 11.3 years, 861 bladder cancer cases were identified.

effect_size.excerpt: Gender-specific analysis showed that a higher intake of monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) was linked to a reduced risk of bladder cancer in females (HR: 0.62; 95% CI: 0.39-0.99, P-trend = 0.028). However, restricted cubic spline analysis revealed no linear relationship between MUFA intake and bladder cancer risk in the overall group or gender-specific subgroups.

confidence_interval.excerpt: Gender-specific analysis showed that a higher intake of monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) was linked to a reduced risk of bladder cancer in females (HR: 0.62; 95% CI: 0.39-0.99, P-trend = 0.028).

design.excerpt: A quantitative analysis was conducted using data from the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian (PLCO) Cancer Screening Trial
